practice_questions.text:
Which flowchart symbol is used to represent a decision in an algorithm?
A) Rectangle
B) Oval
C) Diamond
D) Parallelogram
practice_questions.marks: C) Diamond [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the pseudocode keyword used to receive input from a user.
practice_questions.marks: INPUT [1 mark] (accept any clear input keyword, e.g. READ)

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'algorithm'.
practice_questions.marks: A precise / step-by-step [1] set of instructions for solving a problem [1]. Award both marks for a definition that captures precision and problem-solving purpose.

practice_questions.text:
The algorithm below is intended to output the sum of all whole numbers from 1 to 5.

SET total = 0
FOR i = 1 TO 5
  SET total = total + i
NEXT i
OUTPUT total

Complete a trace table showing the value of i and total after each iteration of the loop.
practice_questions.marks:
Full trace table:
i=1, total=1 [1]
i=2, total=3 [1]
i=3, total=6 [1]
i=4, total=10; i=5, total=15; OUTPUT 15 [1]
Mastering: All rows correct with output 15.
Secure: 3 out of 4 rows correct.
Developing: 2 correct rows.
Emerging: 1 correct row or only final answer given.

practice_questions.text: A student wants to write a pseudocode algorithm that asks a user for their age and outputs 'Adult' if the age is 18 or over, or 'Minor' if it is below 18. Write a pseudocode algorithm to do this.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Write an Algorithm in Pseudocode
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correct INPUT, valid IF condition (age >= 18), correct THEN/ELSE branches with matching OUTPUT, END IF present, all keywords correct — 5-6 marks.
Secure: Logic correct but minor keyword inconsistency or missing END IF — 3-4 marks.
Developing: IF condition present but branches or keywords incomplete — 2 marks.
Emerging: Some keywords attempted but logic incorrect — 1 mark.
Model answer:
INPUT age
IF age >= 18 THEN
  OUTPUT "Adult"
ELSE
  OUTPUT "Minor"
END IF

practice_questions.text: A programmer designs a flowchart before writing code. Explain two advantages of designing an algorithm using a flowchart before writing code.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks per advantage (1 for the point, 1 for development):
- Visual representation makes the flow of control easy to follow / easier to spot logic errors before any code is written [1+1].
- Language-independent: the flowchart can be converted into any programming language / a team member unfamiliar with Python can still understand the algorithm [1+1].
- Easier to communicate with non-programmers / clients can review logic without needing to read code [1+1].
Mastering: Two distinct, well-developed advantages.
Secure: Two valid advantages, one developed.
Developing: One developed advantage or two simple points.
Emerging: One simple relevant point.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the digital divide?
A) The difference in speed between fibre-optic and copper cable broadband
B) The gap between those who have reliable access to digital technology and those who do not
C) The division between computer hardware and computer software
D) The difference between public and private cloud services
practice_questions.marks: B) The gap between those who have reliable access to digital technology and those who do not [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one toxic substance found in discarded electronic devices that can cause environmental harm.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any one of: lead / mercury / cadmium / lithium [1 mark]. Accept any named toxic substance correctly associated with e-waste.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'AI bias' and explain one way it can cause harm.
practice_questions.marks:
Definition (1 mark): AI bias occurs when an AI system produces unfair or discriminatory outcomes because the training data reflects existing social inequalities.
Explanation of harm (1 mark): for example, a recruitment algorithm trained on historical data may systematically disadvantage candidates from under-represented groups, even when the programmer did not intend this. Accept any clearly stated mechanism of harm.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which automation of jobs by computers has affected society. For each way, consider both the benefit and the drawback.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks, 2 per way.
Way 1 (example): Automation raises productivity and creates new, higher-skilled technology roles (benefit). However, workers in the automated roles — often lower-paid, less-qualified — may lack the skills to move into the new jobs, increasing unemployment and inequality (drawback). [2 marks for benefit + drawback with development]
Way 2 (example): Self-checkout machines allow retailers to operate longer hours with fewer staff, reducing costs and prices for consumers (benefit). Staff who lose checkout jobs may struggle to find equivalent pay elsewhere, and vulnerable customers who need assistance are disadvantaged (drawback). [2 marks for benefit + drawback with development]
Accept any two clearly distinct impacts, each with a stated benefit and drawback. [1 mark per way for a simple point only]

practice_questions.text: Describe three environmental impacts of the widespread use of digital technology.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for three distinct impacts. Accept any of:
- E-waste: discarded devices contain toxic materials (lead, mercury, cadmium) that leach into soil and groundwater when landfilled.
- Energy consumption of data centres: data centres powering cloud services and the internet consume large amounts of electricity, contributing to carbon emissions if powered by fossil fuels.
- Manufacturing impact: producing chips, circuit boards and batteries requires rare earth minerals and energy-intensive processes.
- Short device lifespan: rapid replacement cycles mean more waste and resource consumption than if devices lasted longer.
- Cryptocurrency/AI training energy: some computationally intensive processes consume electricity equivalent to small countries.

practice_questions.text:
"The benefits of digital technology to society outweigh its negative impacts."
Discuss this statement. In your answer, consider ethical, cultural and environmental impacts of digital technology, and reach an overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Considers at least three distinct impact types (e.g. privacy, digital divide, e-waste) with specific evidence for each. Each point includes a clear counter-argument. Reaches a supported overall conclusion that justifies a view using the evidence presented. Writing is coherent and well-structured.
Secure (5-6 marks): Covers at least two impact types with some development on both sides. A conclusion is present but may lack full justification.
Developing (3-4 marks): Identifies impacts but treats them one-sidedly (all positives or all negatives). Some attempt at balance but no conclusion, or conclusion not supported by argument.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Simple list of impacts with no development or balance. No conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the correct data type for the value 3.75?
A) Integer
B) Boolean
C) Real
D) Character
practice_questions.marks: C) Real [1 mark]. 3.75 has a fractional part so it cannot be an integer; Boolean is only True/False; Character is a single symbol.

practice_questions.text: State the denary value of the binary number 01101010.
practice_questions.marks: 64 + 32 + 8 + 2 = 106. [2 marks: 1 mark for correct method shown (column headers or repeated halving), 1 mark for correct answer 106. Accept answer-only for full marks if correct.]

practice_questions.text: Convert the denary number 219 into hexadecimal. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 219 = 13 × 16 + 11 = DB in hex. [2 marks: 1 mark for correct binary or correct individual nibble, 1 mark for correct final hex DB. Accept working via binary: 11011011 → 1101 1011 → D B.]

practice_questions.text: A programmer needs to store a student's exam score out of 100, their name, and whether they passed or failed. Identify the most appropriate data type for each of the three values.
practice_questions.marks: Exam score → Integer (whole number, no decimal needed). Name → String (sequence of characters). Passed/failed → Boolean (only two possible values: True or False). [1 mark each, 3 marks total.]

practice_questions.text: Explain why hexadecimal is used by programmers as a shorthand for binary rather than denary.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for points such as: One hex digit represents exactly four binary bits (a nibble) [1], so conversion between hex and binary is fast and reliable without arithmetic [1]; an 8-bit byte needs only two hex digits, whereas the denary equivalent can be up to three digits and requires calculation to convert [1]; this makes hex useful for representing memory addresses, colour codes and error codes in a compact, readable form [1]. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Compare the integer and real data types. In your answer, refer to how each is stored and when each should be chosen.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate contrast of storage (integer stored as fixed binary pattern; real stored using floating-point with sign, mantissa and exponent), clear examples of when each is appropriate (integer for counts/IDs; real for measurements/currency), and a comparison of storage efficiency (integer typically uses fewer bytes than real for the same range).
Secure: Correct definitions of both types, at least one storage difference explained, and appropriate use cases given.
Developing: Definitions correct but comparison is implicit (e.g. lists integer facts then real facts without explicitly contrasting them).
Emerging: One type partially described; little or no comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an advantage of a star topology?
A) The network continues to function if the central switch fails
B) Each device has a dedicated link to the switch, so one device's traffic does not slow another
C) It requires less cabling than a bus topology
D) Data travels around a loop, preventing collisions
practice_questions.marks: B) Each device has a dedicated link to the switch, so one device's traffic does not slow another [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one disadvantage of using a bus topology in a school network.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for any one of:
- If the backbone cable fails, the entire network stops working.
- Only one device can transmit at a time; heavy traffic causes collisions.
- Performance degrades as more devices are added. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two characteristics of a mesh topology.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
- Each device connects to multiple other devices, creating redundant paths for data. [1]
- If one path fails, data is automatically rerouted, giving high fault tolerance with no single point of failure. [1]
- A full mesh is expensive to cable and complex to configure, especially as the network grows. [1]
[Award up to 3 marks for two clearly described characteristics, with development of at least one.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why a hospital might choose a mesh topology rather than a ring topology for its critical patient-records network.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks (2 marks per reason):
Reason 1: Fault tolerance
- Mesh has no single point of failure because data can reroute through alternative paths. [1]
- In a ring, a single cable or device failure halts the entire network, which is unacceptable in a hospital where access to patient records must be continuous. [1]
Reason 2: Reliability for heavy traffic
- Mesh supports simultaneous data paths, increasing throughput during peak demand. [1]
- In a ring, data must pass through every intermediate device to reach its destination, causing delays when the network is busy. [1]

practice_questions.text:
A small design studio has four computers and a shared printer. They want to connect all devices so that if one computer's cable fails, the others remain connected. They have a limited budget.

Which topology would you recommend? Justify your answer with reference to both fault tolerance and cost.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Recommends star topology with a clear comparison against at least one alternative, explicitly contrasting fault tolerance and cost; concludes with a justified recommendation that accounts for both criteria.
Secure: Recommends star topology with a valid explanation of fault tolerance and cost; comparison with another topology may be implicit rather than explicit.
Developing: Identifies star topology as suitable and gives a reason, but the reasoning is one-sided (only cost or only fault tolerance).
Emerging: Names a topology with limited or no justification.

practice_questions.text:
Discuss the impact of network technology on everyday life.

In your answer, consider both the benefits it brings and the problems it can cause.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument with developed benefits (resource sharing, communication, remote work, access to information) and developed problems (dependency on connectivity, security vulnerabilities, cost of infrastructure, privacy concerns); reaches a reasoned conclusion about overall impact.
Secure: At least two developed benefits and two developed problems; conclusion present but may lack nuance.
Developing: Benefits and problems listed but not equally developed; limited conclusion.
Emerging: Simple points about benefits or problems only; no conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the role of the Control Unit (CU)?
A) It performs arithmetic and logical operations on data
B) It stores the result of the most recent calculation
C) It directs the fetch-decode-execute cycle and sends control signals to other components
D) It holds the address of the next instruction to be fetched
practice_questions.marks: C) It directs the fetch-decode-execute cycle and sends control signals to other components [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the purpose of the Accumulator (ACC) in a CPU.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: holds the result of the most recent ALU operation / stores the output of arithmetic or logical calculations / acts as the working register for ALU results. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'Von Neumann architecture'.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks: 1 mark for identifying that instructions and data are stored in the same memory; 1 mark for identifying that the CPU fetches, decodes and executes instructions in sequence from that shared memory. Do not award for a description that only mentions one of the two key points.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between the Memory Address Register (MAR) and the Memory Data Register (MDR). Use an example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• MAR holds the address in memory that the CPU is currently accessing (reading from or writing to). [1 mark]
• MDR holds the actual data that has been fetched from that address, or the data about to be written to it. [1 mark]
• Clear contrast: MAR contains an address (a location), MDR contains a value (the content of that location). [1 mark]
• Relevant example, e.g. when fetching an instruction, the address of that instruction is placed in the MAR; the instruction itself is then copied into the MDR. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Compare the roles of cache memory and RAM in a Von Neumann computer system.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for explicit comparisons:
• Unlike RAM, which stores all currently running programs and data, cache stores only a small subset of frequently used or recently accessed instructions. [1 mark per comparative point, up to 3 distinct comparisons]
• Cache is faster than RAM because it is located on or very close to the CPU die; RAM is a separate component connected via the memory bus.
• Cache is much smaller in capacity (L1: 32–64 KB; L3: up to ~32 MB) compared to typical RAM (8–32 GB on a modern PC).
• Both are volatile — both lose their contents when power is removed.
• Cache reduces CPU stall time by supplying instructions without requiring a RAM access; RAM cannot do this because of the slower access time over the memory bus.
Mastering: Four or more clearly stated contrasts with precise technical detail.
Secure: Three clear contrasts with some technical detail.
Developing: Two contrasts, one or both lacking precision.
Emerging: Features of one component listed without comparison.

practice_questions.text: A student says: 'The Control Unit processes all data in a computer.' Explain why this statement is incorrect and describe which component carries out this role instead.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• The statement is incorrect because the CU does not process data. [1 mark]
• The CU manages and coordinates the fetch-decode-execute cycle, sending control signals to other components. [1 mark]
• Data processing (arithmetic and logical operations) is carried out by the ALU. [1 mark]
• The ALU receives values from registers (e.g. the ACC), performs the required operation, and stores the result back in a register. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the output of an XOR gate?
A) Outputs 1 when both inputs are 1
B) Outputs 1 when at least one input is 1
C) Outputs 1 when the two inputs are different
D) Outputs 1 when both inputs are 0
practice_questions.marks: C) Outputs 1 when the two inputs are different [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the Boolean notation symbol used to represent the AND operator.
practice_questions.marks: A dot (·) or placing letters side by side, e.g. A·B or AB [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Complete the truth table below for the expression NOT A AND B.

A | B | NOT A | NOT A AND B
0 | 0 |       |
0 | 1 |       |
1 | 0 |       |
1 | 1 |       |
practice_questions.marks:
NOT A column: 1, 1, 0, 0 [1 mark]
NOT A AND B column: 0, 1, 0, 0 [1 mark]
Both marks awarded independently per column.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between an OR gate and an XOR gate. Use a truth table row to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: OR outputs 1 when at least one input is 1 [1]; this includes the case where both inputs are 1 [1]. XOR outputs 1 only when the inputs are different [1]; when both inputs are 1, XOR outputs 0 [1]. The key distinguishing row is (1,1): OR gives 1, XOR gives 0.

practice_questions.text: A security system uses two sensors, A and B. The alarm triggers (output = 1) only when both sensors detect a problem at the same time. Identify which logic gate models this behaviour and complete a full truth table for it.
practice_questions.marks: Gate identified as AND [1]. Truth table with four rows: (0,0) gives 0, (0,1) gives 0, (1,0) gives 0, (1,1) gives 1 [1 mark per correct row up to 3 marks]. Full marks: all four rows correct and AND identified.

practice_questions.text: Compare how a NAND gate and a NOR gate behave. In your answer, relate each gate to its component parts and explain when each outputs a 0.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: NAND described as AND then NOT — outputs 0 only when both inputs are 1 (unlike AND which outputs 1); NOR described as OR then NOT — outputs 1 only when both inputs are 0; explicit contrast of the two (e.g. unlike NAND, which outputs 0 only in the row where both inputs are 1, NOR outputs 0 in three of four rows); conclusion that both are universal gates.
Secure: Both gates correctly described with their component parts; comparison present but may lack one explicit contrast point.
Developing: One gate correctly described or one contrast made without full explanation.
Emerging: Partial attempt; may confuse NAND with NOR or omit the NOT stage.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes what happens to the Program Counter during the Fetch stage?
A) It is reset to zero after each instruction
B) It is incremented to point to the next instruction's address
C) It is copied into the Accumulator
D) It stores the instruction being decoded
practice_questions.marks: B) It is incremented to point to the next instruction's address [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the name of the register that holds the instruction currently being decoded.
practice_questions.marks: Current Instruction Register (CIR). [1 mark — both expanded name and abbreviation acceptable]

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during the Fetch stage of the FDE cycle. Refer to the registers used in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for three of the following:
• The address in the PC is copied into the MAR.
• The PC is incremented (to point to the next instruction).
• The instruction is retrieved from RAM (at the address held in the MAR) into the MDR.
• The instruction is copied from the MDR into the CIR.

practice_questions.text: Explain how increasing the clock speed of a CPU improves its performance. Include one disadvantage of using a very high clock speed.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Clock speed measures the number of FDE cycles per second. [1 mark]
• A higher clock speed means more instructions are executed every second, so programs run faster. [1 mark]
• Disadvantage: higher clock speed generates more heat, which requires more cooling and may cause the processor to throttle (reduce speed) to avoid damage. [1 mark]
• Additional relevant point, e.g. higher clock speed increases power consumption. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Compare the effect of increasing the number of CPU cores with increasing the clock speed as methods of improving CPU performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for explicit, comparative points:
• Both increasing clock speed and adding cores can improve overall processing throughput, but by different mechanisms.
• Clock speed increases the rate at which each core processes instructions — all programs benefit regardless of how they are written.
• Unlike clock speed, adding cores only benefits programs written to use multiple threads (parallel execution); a single-threaded program runs on one core only.
• Increasing clock speed generates more heat; adding cores increases power consumption and chip area but less dramatically per core.
• A processor with more cores may outperform a higher-clock-speed processor for multitasking (e.g. running many applications simultaneously) but underperform for a single demanding serial task.
Mastering: Four or more clearly contrasted comparative points with specific technical detail.
Secure: Three clear contrasts.
Developing: Two comparisons, one or both lacking precision.
Emerging: Features of clock speed or cores listed without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Explain the role of cache memory in improving CPU performance. In your answer, explain what happens when a 'cache miss' occurs.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Cache stores frequently used or recently accessed instructions and data close to the CPU. [1 mark]
• When the CPU needs data it first checks cache (cache hit); if found, it can proceed immediately without waiting for RAM. [1 mark]
• A cache miss occurs when the required data is not in cache; the CPU must fetch it from RAM, which is significantly slower. [1 mark]
• This stall time reduces performance; a larger cache reduces the frequency of cache misses and so improves overall CPU speed. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Which construct is used when a block of code must be repeated a fixed, known number of times?
A) Sequence
B) Selection
C) Count-controlled iteration
D) Condition-controlled iteration
practice_questions.marks: C) Count-controlled iteration [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a 'rogue value' in the context of a condition-controlled loop.
practice_questions.marks: A special/agreed value entered by the user to signal that data entry should stop [1 mark]. Accept 'sentinel value'.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between a local variable and a global variable.
practice_questions.marks:
Local variable: declared inside a subroutine [1], only accessible within that subroutine / destroyed when the subroutine ends [1].
Global variable: declared outside all subroutines [1], accessible from anywhere in the program / exists for the program's lifetime [1].
Mastering: Both definitions with scope clearly contrasted.
Secure: Both definitions present, contrast implied.
Developing: One correct definition.
Emerging: Vague reference to variables without scope distinction.

practice_questions.text: Write a pseudocode algorithm that uses a WHILE loop to keep asking the user to enter a positive number until they enter -1 (the rogue value), then outputs the count of numbers entered (not including -1).
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Write an Algorithm in Pseudocode
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Correct INPUT before loop, WHILE condition checking for -1, counter incremented inside loop, second INPUT inside loop, OUTPUT count after loop — 5-6 marks.
Secure: Logic correct but minor issue (e.g. counter initialisation missing) — 3-4 marks.
Developing: Loop structure present but condition or counter flawed — 2 marks.
Emerging: Some relevant keywords used — 1 mark.
Model:
SET count = 0
INPUT number
WHILE number <> -1
  SET count = count + 1
  INPUT number
END WHILE
OUTPUT count

practice_questions.text:
A student writes the following Python function:

def multiply(a, b):
    result = a * b
    return result

Identify whether 'result' is a local or global variable and explain why.
practice_questions.marks:
'result' is a local variable [1] because it is declared inside the function 'multiply' [1] and cannot be accessed from outside the function [1]. When the function finishes executing, 'result' is destroyed [1].
Mastering: Correct classification with two valid reasons.
Secure: Correct classification with one reason.
Developing: Correct classification without explanation.
Emerging: Partial or incorrect response.

practice_questions.text: Compare the use of a WHILE loop and a REPEAT...UNTIL loop. Include in your answer when each type would be more appropriate to use.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At least two explicit contrasts, each identifying the key difference (pre-condition vs post-condition) and linking it to an appropriate scenario — 5-6 marks.
Secure: One explicit contrast with scenario, one further point — 3-4 marks.
Developing: Correct description of one loop type — 2 marks.
Emerging: A relevant point about loops — 1 mark.
Points may include:
- WHILE checks condition before executing the body (pre-condition); if condition is already false, the body never runs. REPEAT...UNTIL checks after the body runs (post-condition), so the body always executes at least once.
- WHILE is appropriate when the loop might not need to run at all (e.g. if the list is already empty). REPEAT...UNTIL is appropriate for input validation where you always need at least one prompt.
- Both are condition-controlled; unlike FOR they do not need a known number of repetitions in advance.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the 8-bit two's complement representation of -13?
A) 10001101
B) 11110011
C) 01110011
D) 11110010
State what is meant by overflow in the context of binary addition.
practice_questions.marks: Overflow occurs when the result of an addition is too large to be stored in the available number of bits [1 mark]. Accept: the result exceeds the maximum value the bit width can represent, causing the value to wrap around or be recorded incorrectly.

practice_questions.text: Convert the 8-bit two's complement number 11001010 to its denary value.
practice_questions.marks: MSB is 1, so the number is negative. Invert: 00110101. Add 1: 00110110 = 54. Therefore the denary value is -54. [2 marks: 1 mark for correct invert-and-add-1 process, 1 mark for correct answer -54.]

practice_questions.text: Carry out the binary addition of 01011001 and 00110111. Show your working. State whether overflow has occurred if the result is to be stored as an 8-bit unsigned integer.
practice_questions.marks: 01011001 + 00110111: working column by column with carries gives 10010000, which is 128 + 16 = 144 in denary. [1 mark for correct carry work, 1 mark for result 10010000, 1 mark for correctly stating 144 is within the 0-255 unsigned range, 1 mark for concluding no overflow in unsigned 8-bit.]

practice_questions.text: The 8-bit binary value 00011000 is stored in a register. Show the result of an arithmetic right shift by 2 positions and state the denary value of the result.
practice_questions.marks: 00011000 shifted right 2 positions arithmetically (sign bit 0, so 0s fill from left): 00000110. [1 mark for correct shift direction with two positions, 1 mark for correct result 00000110, 1 mark for correct denary value 6.] Note: equivalent to dividing 24 by 4.

practice_questions.text: Compare sign and magnitude with two's complement as methods of representing negative integers in binary. In your answer, refer to the range of values each can represent and how each handles the representation of zero.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate contrast of range (sign and magnitude: -127 to +127 in 8 bits; two's complement: -128 to +127 in 8 bits), clear explanation of the double-zero problem in sign and magnitude vs single zero in two's complement, and a comment on why two's complement is preferred by hardware (same addition circuit works for subtraction).
Secure: Both representations described correctly, at least one contrast made explicitly (e.g. range or zero), some comment on hardware implications.
Developing: One representation described well; the other partially correct; comparison implicit rather than explicit.
Emerging: Some correct facts about one representation; little or no comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an offence under the Computer Misuse Act 1990?
A) Failing to register personal data with the Information Commissioner's Office
B) Accessing a computer system without authorisation
C) Sharing copyrighted music with attribution to the original artist
D) Refusing to respond to a Freedom of Information request within 20 days
practice_questions.marks: B) Accessing a computer system without authorisation [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the year in which the Computer Misuse Act was passed.
Define the term 'Subject Access Request' and state which piece of legislation gives individuals this right.
practice_questions.marks:
Subject Access Request (1 mark): a formal request made by an individual to an organisation asking for a copy of all personal data held about them.
Legislation (1 mark): the Data Protection Act 2018 (also accept: UK GDPR).

practice_questions.text: Explain two rights that individuals have under the Data Protection Act 2018.
practice_questions.marks:
2 marks per right (1 mark for naming the right, 1 mark for a clear explanation of what it allows).
Right 1 examples:
- Right of access / Subject Access Request: individuals can request a copy of all personal data an organisation holds about them. [2]
- Right to erasure: individuals can ask an organisation to delete their personal data in certain circumstances, sometimes called the right to be forgotten. [2]
- Right to rectification: individuals can demand that inaccurate data about them is corrected. [2]
- Right to data portability: individuals can request their data in a machine-readable format to transfer to another service. [2]
Must name two distinct rights, each with a correct explanation.

practice_questions.text: Describe three ways that the Regulation of Investigatory Powers Act 2000 (RIPA) affects how public bodies can monitor individuals online.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for three correct points. Accept any of:
- RIPA requires that surveillance by public bodies (police, intelligence services) must be authorised before it takes place.
- Authorisations must be necessary and proportionate to the suspected offence or threat.
- Police can request an ISP to retain records of a suspect's internet activity, but only with proper authorisation.
- Without authorisation, accessing a person's communications data is unlawful under RIPA.
- RIPA was later extended by the Investigatory Powers Act 2016, which provides for bulk data collection by intelligence services.
Do not award marks for describing the Data Protection Act or Freedom of Information Act.

practice_questions.text:
"Professional codes of conduct are unnecessary because the law already sets out what computing professionals must do."
Discuss this statement. In your answer, consider the purpose of both legislation and professional codes of conduct for people working in computing.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): Clearly distinguishes between legislation (minimum standard, externally enforced, criminal/civil sanctions) and professional codes (go further, set positive standards, backed by professional body discipline). At least two developed points on each side with specific examples (e.g. BCS Code of Conduct obligations, what CMA/DPA require). Reaches a supported conclusion, e.g. that codes are necessary because laws address specific offences but cannot anticipate every ethical dilemma a professional will face. Writing is coherent.
Secure (5-6 marks): Covers both sides with some development. Conclusion present but may be limited.
Developing (3-4 marks): Identifies one or two points on each side but development is thin. Conclusion absent or not supported.
Emerging (1-2 marks): Simple list of points about laws or codes; no balance or conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
Which Boolean algebra law states that A + A = A?
A) Identity
B) Complement
C) Idempotent
D) Annulment
practice_questions.marks: C) Idempotent [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State De Morgan's first law in words.
practice_questions.marks: NOT(A AND B) equals NOT A OR NOT B [1 mark]. Accept equivalent overbar notation.

practice_questions.text: Simplify the Boolean expression A·1 + A·NOT(A), showing the law used at each step.
practice_questions.marks: Step 1: Identity law — A·1 = A; expression becomes A + A·NOT(A) [1]. Step 2: Complement law — A·NOT(A) = 0; expression becomes A + 0 [1]. Step 3: Identity law (OR form) — A + 0 = A [1]. Final answer: A [1]. Award each mark for the correct application of the named law.

practice_questions.text: Simplify the Boolean expression NOT(A OR B) OR A, showing the law applied at each stage.
practice_questions.marks: Step 1: De Morgan's second law — NOT(A OR B) = NOT A AND NOT B; expression becomes NOT(A)·NOT(B) + A [1]. Step 2: Distributive law — factor (NOT(A) + A)·(NOT(B) + A) or apply Complement to NOT(A) + A = 1 [1]. Step 3: Complement on A + NOT(A) = 1 [1]. Result: NOT(B) + A, reached by Identity because A · 1 = A, or equivalent simplified form [1]. Accept any correct step-by-step route to the correct simplified form.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Absorption law A + A·B = A is true. You may use a truth table to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks: When A = 0: 0 + 0·B = 0 = A for any B [1]. When A = 1: 1 + 1·B = 1 = A for any B [1]. Therefore the B term adds nothing to the result — whenever A is 0 the whole expression is 0, and whenever A is 1 the whole expression is 1 [1]. The expression reduces to A alone [1].

practice_questions.text: A student claims that A·B + A·NOT(B) = A. Show, using Boolean algebra laws, whether this claim is correct.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Step 1 applies Distributive law to factor out A: A·(B + NOT(B)) [law named]; Step 2 applies Complement: B + NOT(B) = 1 [law named]; Step 3 applies Identity: A·1 = A [law named]; conclusion that the claim is correct with all three laws correctly named and applied.
Secure: Correct simplification to A with at least two laws correctly named; minor labelling error in one step.
Developing: Correct simplification shown but fewer than two laws named; or one step skipped.
Emerging: Some attempt to factor the expression; does not reach correct conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the function of a switch?
A) It connects separate networks together using IP addresses
B) It broadcasts incoming data to every connected device
C) It forwards data only to the device it is addressed to, using MAC addresses
D) It allows wireless devices to connect to a wired network
practice_questions.marks: C) It forwards data only to the device it is addressed to, using MAC addresses [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the purpose of a Network Interface Card (NIC).
practice_questions.marks: One mark for: A NIC provides the physical hardware interface that allows a device to connect to a network; it is assigned a unique MAC address at manufacture. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe the difference between a hub and a switch.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
- A hub broadcasts all incoming data to every connected device, regardless of the intended recipient. [1]
- A switch uses a MAC address table to forward data only to the specific destination device. [1]
- This makes switches more efficient (less wasted bandwidth) and more secure (other devices cannot read the data). [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain why a school might install multiple wireless access points (WAPs) throughout its building rather than using a single WAP.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks:
- A single WAP has a limited range, and walls, floors and other physical barriers weaken the wireless signal. [1]
- Placing multiple WAPs throughout the building ensures full coverage so that devices in every room can connect. [1]
- Multiple WAPs can be connected back to the same wired network, so users experience seamless connectivity as they move between areas. [1]
- This also distributes the load across multiple access points, preventing any one WAP from becoming overloaded and slow. [1]

practice_questions.text: A business is upgrading its network. It currently uses hubs throughout the building. Explain two reasons why replacing the hubs with switches would improve the network's performance and security.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two well-developed reasons, each with explicit comparison between hub and switch behaviour; uses precise technical language (MAC address table, broadcast, bandwidth).
Secure: Two valid reasons developed with some technical detail; comparison present but may lack precision in one reason.
Developing: Two reasons identified but at least one underdeveloped; little explicit comparison.
Emerging: One reason given with limited technical detail.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of wireless networking compared to wired networking for a large secondary school.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion with developed advantages of wireless (mobility, flexibility, no cabling cost, easy to add devices) and developed disadvantages (interference, security risks, speed/range limitations) balanced against wired advantages; reaches a justified conclusion appropriate to a school context.
Secure: At least two developed advantages and two developed disadvantages; conclusion present.
Developing: Arguments listed but not equally developed; conclusion limited.
Emerging: Simple statements about one side only.

before.exam_tip_html: A very common exam error is confusing a switch with a hub. Remember: a hub broadcasts data to every device; a switch uses MAC addresses to send data only to the intended device. If a question asks you to “compare a switch and a hub”, you must include an explicit contrast using the words “unlike” or “whereas”. For questions on wired vs wireless, always mention both a technical difference (e.g. speed or interference) and a security difference — examiners reward multi-dimensional comparisons.

practice_questions.text:
A programmer stores the daily temperatures for one week as seven real numbers. Which data structure is most appropriate?
A) Record
B) 2D array
C) 1D array
D) File
practice_questions.marks: C) 1D array [1 mark] — seven values of the same type (real) stored in sequence.

practice_questions.text: State one difference between a 1D array and a record.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: a 1D array stores items of the same data type, whereas a record can store fields of different data types [1]; a 1D array is accessed by a single integer index, whereas a record's fields are accessed by name [1].

practice_questions.text: A school stores the following information about each pupil: pupil ID (string), year group (integer), name (string), and whether they are eligible for free school meals (Boolean). Design a record structure for one pupil, showing the field name and data type for each field.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark per field correctly identified with its data type up to three marks:
• PupilID — String [1]
• YearGroup — Integer [1]
• Name — String (or Surname + Forename as two fields, each String) [1]
• FreeMeals / EligibleFSM — Boolean [1]
Three marks total; accept equivalent field names.

practice_questions.text:
A programmer uses a 2D array called results to store test scores for 4 students, each having 5 test results. Write Python code to:
(a) declare the array with realistic values
(b) print the score of student 2 (0-indexed) in test 4 (0-indexed)
practice_questions.marks: (a) A valid 2D list with 4 rows and 5 columns, e.g. results = [[...],[...],[...],[...]] [2 — 1 for correct structure, 1 for correct dimensions]. (b) print(results[2][4]) [2 — 1 for correct syntax, 1 for correct indices].

practice_questions.text: Explain why a record is a more appropriate data structure than a 1D array when storing information about a library book (title, ISBN, author, number of pages, available).
practice_questions.marks: The fields have different data types: title and author are strings, ISBN is a string, number of pages is an integer, and available is a Boolean [1]. A 1D array can only store one data type [1], so it cannot hold all five fields together [1]. A record allows named fields of different types to represent one entity (one book) [1].

practice_questions.text: A hospital needs to store medical records for 10,000 patients permanently. Each patient record contains: patient ID, surname, forename, date of birth, and blood type. Compare using a 2D array with using a file of records for this purpose.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: 2D array can only hold one data type — cannot store a mix of strings, dates and integers in the same structure; a file of records handles mixed types per patient [contrast made explicitly]; a 2D array is stored in RAM and lost when the program ends, unlike a file which persists on secondary storage; file supports individual record retrieval by ID without loading all data into RAM; conclusion that a file of records is the appropriate choice for permanent multi-type storage at scale.
Secure: Two clear contrasting points made; both structures described correctly; minor omission in conclusion.
Developing: One contrast correctly made (e.g. data types or persistence); second contrast weak or missing.
Emerging: Describes one structure only; no explicit comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a characteristic of RAM?
A) Non-volatile and read-only
B) Volatile and read/write
C) Non-volatile and read/write
D) Volatile and read-only
practice_questions.marks: B) Volatile and read/write [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one advantage of an SSD over an HDD.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: faster access speed / more durable (no moving parts) / silent in operation / lower power consumption. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: A digital photograph is 4,000 pixels wide and 3,000 pixels tall. Each pixel is stored using 24 bits. Calculate the storage required for this image in megabytes (MB). Show your working.
practice_questions.marks:
Step 1: 4,000 × 3,000 × 24 = 288,000,000 bits [1 mark]
Step 2: 288,000,000 ÷ 8 = 36,000,000 bytes [1 mark]
Step 3: 36,000,000 ÷ 1,024 ÷ 1,024 = approximately 34.3 MB [1 mark for correct final answer in MB using base-2]
Note: answers using base-10 (36,000,000 ÷ 1,000,000 = 36 MB) do not receive the unit-conversion mark.

practice_questions.text: Explain the purpose of virtual memory and describe one disadvantage of using it.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Virtual memory is a section of secondary storage used as an extension of RAM when physical RAM is full. [1 mark]
• The operating system moves sections of RAM that have not been recently used to the secondary storage page file, freeing RAM for the currently active task. [1 mark]
• Disadvantage: secondary storage (e.g. HDD or SSD) is much slower than RAM, so relying on virtual memory causes a noticeable slowdown in system performance. [1 mark]
• Additional relevant point, e.g. if virtual memory is used heavily it can cause 'thrashing' — the OS spends more time swapping data than running programs. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Compare magnetic hard disk drives (HDDs) with solid-state drives (SSDs) using the criteria: speed, durability and cost.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks (2 marks per criterion — 1 for each storage type, with an explicit contrast):
Speed: SSDs are significantly faster than HDDs because they use flash memory with no moving parts; HDDs rely on a spinning platter and moving read/write head, introducing mechanical delay (seek time and rotational latency).
Durability: SSDs are more durable because they have no mechanical components that can break or wear out; HDDs contain spinning platters and moving heads that can be damaged by physical shock.
Cost: HDDs are cheaper per gigabyte than SSDs and are therefore preferred when large capacity storage is needed at low cost; SSDs cost more per GB but the price gap has narrowed.
Mastering: All three criteria addressed with clear, explicit contrasts and precise technical vocabulary.
Secure: Two or three criteria addressed with clear contrasts but limited technical detail.
Developing: One or two criteria compared, but contrasts implied rather than explicit.
Emerging: Features of one storage type listed without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of cloud storage compared to local secondary storage for a student storing their school work. Consider at least three criteria in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantages of cloud storage:
• Accessible from any internet-connected device — allows the student to work at home, school and on mobile devices without carrying physical media.
• Effectively unlimited capacity (subscription-based), removing worry about running out of space.
• Files are backed up on remote servers with redundancy, so local hardware failure does not cause data loss.
• Easy to share files with teachers or group members.
Disadvantages of cloud storage:
• Requires a reliable internet connection — files may be inaccessible without internet.
• Security and privacy concerns: files are held by a third party who may be subject to data breaches.
• Ongoing cost: subscription fees apply for large storage quotas.
• Slower access speed than a local SSD if internet bandwidth is limited.
Mastering: Balanced discussion of at least three criteria with explicit advantages AND disadvantages, anchored to the context (student), and a reasoned concluding judgement.
Secure: Three criteria discussed with advantages and disadvantages, but judgement is limited.
Developing: Two criteria discussed; one-sided or limited in context relevance.
Emerging: A list of points without development or explicit criteria.

practice_questions.text:
Which layer of the OSI model is responsible for routing packets across multiple networks using IP addresses?
A) Layer 2 — Data Link
B) Layer 3 — Network
C) Layer 4 — Transport
D) Layer 7 — Application
practice_questions.marks: B) Layer 3 — Network [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the layer of the OSI model at which TCP operates.
practice_questions.marks: Layer 4 — Transport layer. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'protocol' in the context of computer networks.
practice_questions.marks: A protocol is an agreed set of rules [1] that determines how data is formatted and transmitted between devices on a network [1]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the roles of the Presentation layer (layer 6) of the OSI model.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
- Data translation: converts data between different formats or character encodings so that both sender and receiver can interpret it correctly. [1]
- Data compression: reduces the size of data before transmission to increase efficiency. [1]
- Encryption: scrambles data (e.g. using TLS/SSL for HTTPS) so that it cannot be read if intercepted. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between TCP and UDP. Include in your answer an example of an application that uses each protocol and why that protocol is appropriate.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks:
TCP:
- TCP is connection-oriented and guarantees reliable, ordered delivery by acknowledging every segment. [1]
- Example: HTTP (web browsing) — accuracy is essential because a web page with missing data would be unreadable. [1]
UDP:
- UDP is connectionless and sends segments without acknowledgement, making it faster but unreliable. [1]
- Example: video streaming — occasional lost packets cause brief quality drops but retransmitting them would cause buffering, so speed is preferred over perfect reliability. [1]

practice_questions.text:
The OSI model separates network communication into seven layers.

Compare the roles of the Data Link layer (layer 2) and the Network layer (layer 3). In your answer, refer to the addressing method used by each layer and the hardware that operates at each layer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear and explicit comparison of both layers across addressing (MAC vs IP), scope (within one network segment vs across multiple networks), data unit (frame vs packet) and hardware (switch/bridge vs router); language is precise and contrasting throughout.
Secure: Accurate description of both layers with at least two explicit comparisons; may lack one dimension (e.g. hardware).
Developing: Describes one layer well but the comparison is implicit or one-sided.
Emerging: Names the layers or states a fact about one without comparison.

practice_questions.text:
What is the ASCII code for the capital letter 'A'?
A) 48
B) 65
C) 97
D) 64
practice_questions.marks: B) 65 [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a character set.
practice_questions.marks: A character set is a defined collection of characters [1] together with the unique numeric codes assigned to each one, used by a computer to store and display text [1].

practice_questions.text: The character 'Z' has the ASCII code 90. State the ASCII code for the character 'z' and explain how you arrived at your answer.
practice_questions.marks: The ASCII code for 'z' is 122 [1]. The difference between a capital letter and its lower-case equivalent in ASCII is always 32 [1], so 90 + 32 = 122 [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Unicode was developed to replace ASCII.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for points such as: ASCII only supports 128 characters (7-bit), which is sufficient for English but cannot represent characters from other languages such as Chinese, Arabic or Cyrillic [1], making it unsuitable for global software [1]. Extended ASCII introduced additional characters but different manufacturers used the extra 128 codes differently, causing incompatibility between systems [1]. Unicode assigns a unique code point to every character in every writing system, solving both problems with a single consistent standard [1]. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: A student's name is stored in a computer system using ASCII. The name contains 8 characters. Calculate the number of bits needed to store the name.
practice_questions.marks: Each character uses 7 bits in ASCII (or 8 bits as one byte) [1]. Using 8-bit storage (one byte per character): 8 characters × 8 bits = 64 bits [1 mark for method, 1 mark for 64 bits]. If working in 7-bit ASCII: 8 × 7 = 56 bits — accept this with correct working.

practice_questions.text: Compare ASCII and Unicode as methods for storing characters in a computer system. In your answer you should consider the number of characters supported, storage requirements and compatibility.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate contrast of character range (ASCII 128/256 vs Unicode 140,000+), explicit storage comparison (ASCII 1 byte per char; Unicode UTF-8 variable 1-4 bytes), clear statement that UTF-8 is backward compatible with ASCII (first 128 code points match), and a reasoned conclusion about which is preferable and when.
Secure: Both encoding systems described correctly with at least two explicit contrasts; some reference to compatibility.
Developing: One system described well; comparison is mainly implicit; may confuse Unicode the standard with a specific encoding.
Emerging: Some correct facts about one system; little comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following is a requirement for binary search but NOT for linear search?
A) The list must contain integers only
B) The list must be sorted
C) The list must have an odd number of items
D) The list must be stored in a 2D array
practice_questions.marks: B) The list must be sorted [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the maximum number of comparisons needed to search a sorted list of 8 items using binary search.
practice_questions.marks: 3 comparisons [1 mark] — the list halves 8 → 4 → 2 → 1, and log₂ 8 = 3. Accept 4, which also counts the check of the single item left at the end.

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of binary search compared to linear search.
practice_questions.marks:
Advantage: Binary search is much faster on large sorted lists / at most log₂n comparisons vs up to n for linear search [1 + 1 for development].
Disadvantage: Binary search requires the list to be sorted first / if the list changes frequently, re-sorting adds overhead [1 + 1 for development].
Mastering: Both points with development and explicit comparison.
Secure: Both points, one developed.
Developing: One point with development.
Emerging: One valid point.

practice_questions.text:
The sorted list below is searched using binary search for the value 31.
[4, 9, 15, 21, 27, 31, 38, 44]

Complete a trace table showing the values of low, high and mid for each pass, until the target is found.
practice_questions.marks:
Pass 1: low=0, high=7, mid=3, list[3]=21, 31>21 so low=4 [1]
Pass 2: low=4, high=7, mid=5, list[5]=31, match! [1]
Full trace with correct output 'Found at index 5' [1]
All mid calculations correct [1]
Mastering: All rows and output correct.
Secure: 2 rows correct.
Developing: 1 row correct.
Emerging: Correct identification of algorithm type only.

practice_questions.text: Write a pseudocode algorithm for a linear search that searches a list called 'scores' (with 10 items, indices 0 to 9) for a target value entered by the user. Output the index if found or 'Not found' if not.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Write an Algorithm in Pseudocode
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: INPUT target, initialise found/index, correct WHILE loop checking index < 10 AND found = FALSE, IF comparison inside loop, set found = TRUE and output index, post-loop check for not found — 5-6 marks.
Secure: Logic correct, minor issue with loop boundary or keyword — 3-4 marks.
Developing: Loop and IF present but incomplete — 2 marks.
Emerging: INPUT and some loop structure — 1 mark.

practice_questions.text: A school database of 50,000 student records is searched frequently. The records are sorted alphabetically by surname. Discuss whether binary search or linear search would be more suitable, justifying your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Argues binary search is suitable (sorted list meets prerequisite, log₂ 50000 ≈ 16 comparisons vs up to 50000 for linear), develops with efficiency argument, acknowledges linear search as simpler to implement / suitable for unsorted data, reaches a justified conclusion that binary search is preferable for a large, already-sorted dataset.
Secure: Binary search recommended with efficiency justification and acknowledgement of at least one trade-off.
Developing: Correct recommendation, basic efficiency point, limited development.
Emerging: Identifies binary search as faster without justification.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly describes the term 'pixel'?
A) The number of colours an image can contain
B) The smallest addressable element of a digital image, each storing a colour value
C) The file format used to store a bitmap
D) The amount of memory an image uses
practice_questions.marks: B) The smallest addressable element of a digital image, each storing a colour value [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the colour depth of a bitmap image.
practice_questions.marks: The number of bits used to store the colour of a single pixel [1 mark]. Accept: the number of bits per pixel.

practice_questions.text: A bitmap image is 800 pixels wide and 600 pixels tall with a colour depth of 8 bits per pixel. Calculate the uncompressed file size of the image in kilobytes. Show all working.
practice_questions.marks: Step 1: 800 × 600 × 8 = 3,840,000 bits [1 mark for correct multiplication]. Step 2: 3,840,000 ÷ 8 = 480,000 bytes [1 mark]. Step 3: 480,000 ÷ 1024 = 468.75 KB [1 mark — must divide by 1024, not 1000, for this mark]. Accept 468.75 KB or equivalent rounded value with correct method shown.

practice_questions.text: Explain how increasing the colour depth of a bitmap image affects both image quality and file size.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for: Increasing colour depth means more bits are used to represent each pixel [1], so more distinct colours can be stored (e.g. 8-bit gives 256 colours; 24-bit gives over 16 million) [1]. This allows smoother gradients and more accurate colour reproduction, improving image quality [1]. It also increases the file size because more data must be stored for each pixel — a 24-bit image uses three times as much storage as an 8-bit image at the same resolution [1]. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: A student calculates the file size of a 1920 × 1080 image with 24-bit colour as 6,220.8 KB. Identify and correct the error in the student's calculation.
practice_questions.marks: The student divided the bytes by 1000 instead of 1024 [1 mark for identifying the error]. Correct calculation: 1920 × 1080 × 24 = 49,766,400 bits [1]. ÷ 8 = 6,220,800 bytes [1]. ÷ 1024 = 6,075 KB [1 mark for correct final answer using base-2 division]. Accept 5.93 MB (6,075 ÷ 1024) with correct working.

practice_questions.text: Compare the effect of increasing resolution and increasing colour depth on the storage requirements and visual quality of a bitmap image.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both resolution and colour depth increases raise storage proportionally; contrast of effect on quality (resolution affects sharpness/detail; colour depth affects colour accuracy and smoothness of gradients); example calculation values to illustrate; reasoned conclusion about which factor has more impact for a given use case.
Secure: Both factors described correctly, at least one explicit comparison made, correct relationship between factor and file size.
Developing: Both factors mentioned but comparison is implicit or one-sided.
Emerging: One factor partially described.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following correctly describes the worst-case time complexity of bubble sort?
A) O(log n)
B) O(n)
C) O(n log n)
D) O(n²)
practice_questions.marks: D) O(n²) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the two phases of the merge sort algorithm.
practice_questions.marks: Split (divide) phase and merge (combine) phase [1 mark for both named]. Accept 'divide and conquer' as an alternative description.

practice_questions.text:
The following list is to be sorted using bubble sort:
[7, 2, 9, 4, 6]

Show the state of the list after each pass of bubble sort until it is fully sorted. Clearly indicate any swaps made.
practice_questions.marks:
Pass 1: [2, 7, 4, 6, 9] — 7 swaps with 2; 9 swaps with 4 and 6 [1]
Pass 2: [2, 4, 6, 7, 9] — 7 swaps with 4; 7 swaps with 6 [1]
Pass 3: [2, 4, 6, 7, 9] — no swaps, list is sorted [1]
Correct identification that the algorithm terminates after Pass 3 [1]
Mastering: All passes correct with swaps noted.
Secure: Two passes correct.
Developing: One pass correct.
Emerging: Some evidence of comparing adjacent items.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the merge phase of merge sort works, using the example of merging [3, 7] and [1, 5] into a single sorted list.
practice_questions.marks:
Compare the first item of each sub-list [1] — take the smaller (1 from right) [1]. Compare again (3 vs 5) — take 3 [1]. Take 5 then 7 — result [1, 3, 5, 7] [1].
Mastering: Complete merge trace with comparison at each step.
Secure: Three out of four comparison steps correct.
Developing: Process described but trace incomplete.
Emerging: Some reference to comparing items from two lists.

practice_questions.text: A programmer needs to sort a list of 1,000,000 student records. Write an algorithm in pseudocode for bubble sort. Then explain why merge sort would be a more appropriate choice for this task.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Write an Algorithm in Pseudocode
practice_questions.marks:
Pseudocode (3 marks): Outer FOR loop (pass = 1 TO n-1) [1], inner FOR loop (i = 0 TO n-pass-1) [1], IF comparison and three-step swap using temp [1].
Explanation (3 marks): Bubble sort is O(n²) / very slow for 1 million records [1]; merge sort is O(n log n) / significantly faster for large datasets [1]; merge sort's extra memory cost is outweighed by its speed advantage at this scale [1].
Mastering: Correct pseudocode and well-reasoned comparison referencing complexity.
Secure: Correct pseudocode and basic efficiency comparison.
Developing: Pseudocode with errors, or explanation without pseudocode.
Emerging: Some pseudocode keywords or some relevant comparison.

practice_questions.text: Compare bubble sort and merge sort in terms of efficiency and memory use. In your answer, refer to the complexity of each algorithm.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At least two explicit contrasts (efficiency and memory), complexity stated for both (O(n²) vs O(n log n)), scenario discussed (large vs small lists), concluding judgement — 5-6 marks.
Secure: Two contrasts with at least one complexity notation, some context — 3-4 marks.
Developing: One contrast with complexity or two contrasts without — 2 marks.
Emerging: One relevant point — 1 mark.
Points may include: bubble sort O(n²) vs merge sort O(n log n) for large lists; bubble sort is in-place (little extra memory) whereas merge sort needs extra space for merged sub-lists; bubble sort is simpler to implement; merge sort is faster in practice for large datasets.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a dedicated GPU?
A) A graphics processor built into the same chip as the CPU
B) A separate expansion card with its own video memory (VRAM)
C) A component that converts analogue signals to digital data
D) A chip on the motherboard that stores firmware
practice_questions.marks: B) A separate expansion card with its own video memory (VRAM) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the purpose of the data bus on a motherboard.
practice_questions.marks: Carries data between components on the motherboard (e.g. between the CPU and RAM). [1 mark — must reference data transfer; 'connects components' alone is insufficient]

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of a sound card in a computer system.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each for three of the following:
• A sound card converts digital audio data into analogue electrical signals for playback through speakers (DAC).
• It converts analogue signals from a microphone into digital data the computer can process (ADC).
• It handles all audio input and output for the system.
• An integrated sound card is built into the motherboard; a dedicated sound card is a separate expansion card for professional audio use.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a GPU is more suited than a CPU to rendering 3D graphics.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• Rendering 3D graphics requires calculating the colour and position of each pixel independently, which means the same calculation must be done millions of times simultaneously. [1 mark]
• A GPU contains thousands of smaller cores that can perform these calculations in parallel. [1 mark]
• A CPU has fewer, more powerful cores optimised for serial (sequential) tasks, not parallel processing of the same calculation. [1 mark]
• Therefore, a GPU can render complex frames in real time while a CPU would take far longer to produce the same output. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Compare an integrated GPU with a dedicated GPU. Consider performance, power consumption and cost in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for explicit comparisons:
Performance: A dedicated GPU has its own VRAM and is significantly more powerful for graphically demanding tasks (e.g. gaming, video editing); an integrated GPU shares main RAM and performs less well under heavy graphical workloads.
Power consumption: An integrated GPU consumes less power because it shares the CPU’s existing circuits and uses no additional power for separate VRAM; a dedicated GPU requires its own power supply connector and generates significantly more heat.
Cost: An integrated GPU adds little extra cost because it is manufactured on the same chip as the CPU; a dedicated GPU is a separate component that can cost hundreds of pounds.
Mastering: All three criteria addressed with clear, explicitly contrasted comparisons.
Secure: Two or three criteria compared but one lacks precision.
Developing: Features listed for each type without explicit comparison.
Emerging: One criterion partially addressed.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the impact of including a dedicated GPU in a computer system rather than relying on an integrated GPU. Consider the benefits and drawbacks for different types of users.
practice_questions.marks:
Benefits of a dedicated GPU:
• Significantly faster rendering for 3D games, video editing and CAD software.
• Its own VRAM frees up main RAM for other processes, improving multitasking performance.
• Enables use for general-purpose GPU computing (AI, scientific simulation, cryptocurrency).
• Supports multiple high-resolution monitors simultaneously.
Drawbacks of a dedicated GPU:
• Substantially higher cost — from around £100 for basic models to over £1,000 for high-end cards.
• Greater power consumption increases electricity costs and requires a more powerful (and expensive) power supply unit.
• Generates more heat, requiring better case cooling.
• Occupies a PCIe slot and adds physical bulk — not suitable for thin laptops.
User context:
• A gamer or video editor benefits greatly from a dedicated GPU.
• An office worker or student doing word processing or browsing has no practical benefit.
Mastering: Balanced discussion with at least three benefits and three drawbacks, anchored to specific user types, with a reasoned concluding judgement.
Secure: Three points on each side with some user context; judgement present but brief.
Developing: Two points per side; limited user context.
Emerging: One-sided list with no judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following fields in a packet header prevents a packet from circulating the network indefinitely?
A) Source IP address
B) Sequence number
C) Time to Live (TTL)
D) Checksum
practice_questions.marks: C) Time to Live (TTL) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two pieces of information stored in a packet header.
practice_questions.marks: One mark for any two of: source IP address, destination IP address, sequence number, TTL, checksum. [1 mark for two correct fields named]

practice_questions.text: Describe how packet switching allows a large file to be sent across a network.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
- The file is broken into smaller units called packets, each with a header containing addressing and sequencing information. [1]
- Each packet travels independently through the network and may take a different route to the destination. [1]
- At the destination, the packets are reassembled in the correct order using the sequence numbers in their headers. [1]

practice_questions.text:
A network has five routers: P, Q, R, S and T. A packet needs to travel from P to T. The link costs are:
P to Q: 5
P to R: 2
Q to T: 3
R to S: 4
R to Q: 1
S to T: 2

Calculate the cost of each possible route from P to T and state which route a router would choose.
practice_questions.marks:
Routes and costs:
- P → Q → T: 5 + 3 = 8 [1]
- P → R → Q → T: 2 + 1 + 3 = 6 [1]
- P → R → S → T: 2 + 4 + 2 = 8 [1]
Chosen route: P → R → Q → T with a total cost of 6 (lowest). [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain the advantages of packet switching over circuit switching for sending data across a wide area network such as the internet.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explicit comparison of packet switching and circuit switching across at least three dimensions (resilience/fault tolerance, efficient use of bandwidth, cost, scalability); includes specific examples and a conclusion about why packet switching suits the internet.
Secure: At least two advantages of packet switching developed with comparison against circuit switching; conclusion present.
Developing: Two advantages described but comparison is implicit; limited conclusion.
Emerging: One advantage mentioned with no comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Discuss the impact of the internet's use of packet switching on businesses and individuals.

Consider both the benefits and the problems that arise.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument with developed benefits (global communication, resilience, cost efficiency, scalability for e-commerce, remote working) and developed problems (packet loss causing quality issues, security vulnerabilities as packets can be intercepted, reliance on infrastructure, latency in time-critical applications); reasoned conclusion.
Secure: At least two developed benefits and two developed problems; conclusion present.
Developing: Arguments listed without equal development; limited conclusion.
Emerging: Simple points on one side only.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the role of the OS kernel?
A) To provide a user interface for browsing files
B) To manage hardware resources with the highest level of system privilege
C) To scan files for virus signatures
D) To compress files into archives
practice_questions.marks: B) To manage hardware resources with the highest level of system privilege [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a 'device driver'.
practice_questions.marks: Software that allows the OS to communicate with a specific hardware peripheral / translates OS commands into device-specific signals [1 mark].

practice_questions.text: Describe how the OS uses virtual memory when RAM is full.
practice_questions.marks: The OS divides RAM into fixed-size blocks called pages [1]. Inactive pages are moved from RAM to an area of secondary storage called the backing store [1]. When those pages are needed again, they are swapped back into RAM, allowing programs to run even when their total memory demand exceeds installed RAM [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between round-robin scheduling and First-Come-First-Served (FCFS) scheduling.
practice_questions.marks: Round-robin gives each process a fixed time slice (quantum) in turn [1]; when the quantum expires the next process runs, ensuring no process monopolises the CPU [1]. FCFS runs each process to completion in the order it arrives [1]; a long process arriving first can delay all shorter processes behind it [1].

practice_questions.text: Explain why a disk defragmenter is not needed on a solid-state drive (SSD).
practice_questions.marks: Defragmentation reorganises fragmented files into contiguous sectors to reduce mechanical read-head movement [1]. SSDs have no moving parts — they use flash memory chips accessed electronically [1]. Access time is the same regardless of where data is stored on an SSD [1], so defragmentation provides no speed benefit and unnecessarily wears out the flash cells [1].

practice_questions.text: Discuss the benefits and drawbacks of using backup software to protect personal data. In your answer, consider both full and incremental backups.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Benefits clearly developed — data can be restored after accidental deletion, hardware failure or ransomware attack; full backup guarantees a complete copy independent of prior backups; incremental backup saves storage space and time by copying only changed files. Drawbacks developed — full backup requires large storage and takes time; incremental relies on a chain of backups (if one is corrupted, later ones may fail); cloud backup requires bandwidth and raises privacy concerns if data is sensitive. Counter-argument considered: backups use storage resources and must be tested regularly to verify they work. Conclusion presents a reasoned judgement (e.g. the benefits outweigh the cost for critical data, but backup strategy must be tailored to data value and recovery needs).
Secure: At least two benefits and two drawbacks given with development; conclusion present but not fully justified.
Developing: One benefit and one drawback; minimal development; conclusion weak or missing.
Emerging: Only benefits or only drawbacks listed without development.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the best example of an embedded system?
A) A laptop computer running a web browser
B) A microcontroller inside a washing machine controlling the wash cycle
C) A desktop computer running a word processor
D) A server computer managing a school network
practice_questions.marks: B) A microcontroller inside a washing machine controlling the wash cycle [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State one characteristic of an embedded system.
practice_questions.marks: Any one of: dedicated/single function; real-time operation; low power consumption; low cost; high reliability; compact size. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe two characteristics of embedded systems, using an example device for each.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark for each characteristic correctly described, plus 1 further mark for a relevant example that supports both descriptions (or 1 example per characteristic). Max 3:
• Dedicated function: an embedded system is designed to perform one specific task — e.g. a microwave’s controller only manages heating cycles.
• Real-time operation: the system must respond to inputs within a guaranteed time — e.g. an ABS controller must detect wheel lock-up and respond within milliseconds.
• Low power: designed to use minimal power, often battery-powered — e.g. a fitness band must run for days on a small battery.
• High reliability: must not crash because the device may be safety-critical — e.g. a pacemaker cannot be rebooted.

practice_questions.text: Explain why a traffic light control system is an example of an embedded system. Refer to at least two characteristics in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 4 marks:
• A traffic light controller has a dedicated function — it only manages traffic signal timing at a junction; it cannot be used for other purposes. [1 mark]
• It operates in real time — it must change lights in response to road sensor inputs (e.g. detecting waiting vehicles) within a fixed time period to keep traffic flowing safely. [1 mark]
• It is built into the traffic light hardware rather than being a separate general-purpose computer. [1 mark]
• It typically runs continuously without user interaction, demonstrating low power consumption and high reliability. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Compare embedded systems with general-purpose computers. Consider purpose, user interface and cost in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 6 marks for explicit comparisons (2 per criterion):
Purpose: An embedded system is dedicated to a single specific task (e.g. a washing machine controller only manages wash cycles); a general-purpose computer can run any installed software and switch between tasks freely.
User interface: Embedded systems have a minimal interface (a few buttons, LEDs or a small display); a general-purpose computer has a full keyboard, mouse and large display to support varied user interaction.
Cost: Embedded systems use cheap microcontrollers and are produced in huge volumes, making them cost pence to a few pounds per unit; a general-purpose computer costs hundreds to thousands of pounds.
Mastering: All three criteria addressed with clear, explicit contrasts and technical vocabulary.
Secure: Three criteria compared, one or two with limited technical detail.
Developing: Two criteria compared; one lacks an explicit contrast.
Emerging: Features of one type listed without comparison.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the impacts of embedded systems becoming increasingly common in everyday devices such as household appliances, healthcare devices and vehicles. Consider both benefits and potential concerns.
practice_questions.marks:
Benefits:
• Automation and convenience: tasks such as washing cycles and central heating are managed automatically without user input, saving time and reducing effort.
• Improved safety: ABS prevents skids; airbag controllers trigger in milliseconds; smoke detectors detect fire; all improve personal safety.
• Healthcare improvements: pacemakers regulate heart rhythms; insulin pumps deliver precise medication doses; wearables monitor vital signs, enabling early detection of health issues.
• Energy efficiency: smart thermostats and appliances optimise energy use, reducing electricity bills and carbon emissions.
Concerns:
• Security vulnerabilities: internet-connected embedded systems (smart home devices, connected cars) can be hacked, raising privacy and safety risks.
• Reliability in safety-critical applications: a software bug in a pacemaker or car ABS system could endanger life; testing demands are extremely high.
• Environmental impact: billions of embedded chips require rare materials to manufacture and contribute to electronic waste.
• Skill dependency and loss of manual skill: people may lose the ability to perform tasks (e.g. parallel parking) that embedded systems now handle automatically.
Mastering: Balanced discussion of at least three benefits and three concerns, anchored to specific real-world contexts, with a reasoned judgement about overall impact.
Secure: Three points per side with some context; judgement present but limited.
Developing: Two points per side; limited context or one-sided.
Emerging: Unbalanced list with no judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following describes the sample rate of a digital audio recording?
A) The number of bits used to store each measurement of the sound wave
B) The number of times per second the amplitude of the sound wave is measured
C) The number of audio channels recorded simultaneously
