D) The total number of samples in the audio file
practice_questions.marks: B) The number of times per second the amplitude of the sound wave is measured [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the unit used to measure sample rate.
practice_questions.marks: Hertz (Hz) [1 mark]. Accept kHz or kilohertz with correct conversion stated.

practice_questions.text: A mono audio recording is made at a sample rate of 22,050 Hz with a bit depth of 16 bits. The recording lasts 60 seconds. Calculate the uncompressed file size in kilobytes. Show all working.
practice_questions.marks: 22,050 × 16 × 1 × 60 = 21,168,000 bits [1 mark]. ÷ 8 = 2,646,000 bytes [1 mark]. ÷ 1024 = 2,584.0 KB (approximately 2,584 KB) [1 mark — must use 1024 not 1000 for this mark].

practice_questions.text: Explain how increasing the bit depth of a sound recording affects the quality of the audio and the size of the file.
practice_questions.marks: Award marks for: Increasing bit depth means each sample stores more amplitude levels (e.g. 16-bit gives 65,536 levels vs 8-bit giving 256) [1]. This reduces quantisation error — the difference between the actual and stored amplitude values [1], producing a more accurate, higher-quality reproduction of the original sound [1]. More bits per sample means more data to store, so file size increases proportionally (a 16-bit file is twice the size of an 8-bit file at the same sample rate and duration) [1]. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: A student records a 10-second stereo audio clip at 44,100 Hz with a bit depth of 16 bits. The student then records the same clip again in mono at the same settings. Compare the file sizes of the two recordings.
practice_questions.marks: Stereo file: 44,100 × 16 × 2 × 10 = 14,112,000 bits [1]. Mono file: 44,100 × 16 × 1 × 10 = 7,056,000 bits [1]. The stereo file is exactly twice the size of the mono file [1], because stereo records two independent channels (left and right) simultaneously while mono records a single channel [1]. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Discuss the impact of increasing sample rate and bit depth on the quality and storage requirements of digital audio. In your answer, consider practical limits on quality improvement and storage trade-offs.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion of quality benefits (higher sample rate captures higher frequencies; higher bit depth reduces quantisation error), storage costs (both increase file size proportionally), practical limits (human hearing ceiling ~20 kHz means sample rates beyond ~44.1 kHz yield diminishing returns; similar argument for bit depth beyond 16-bit for consumer audio), and a reasoned conclusion about where the trade-off sits for different use cases (e.g. streaming vs professional studio work).
Secure: Quality and storage impacts addressed for both variables; some attempt at a practical limit or trade-off; a conclusion reached.
Developing: Both variables mentioned; impacts mostly correct but comparison is one-sided or limits not addressed.
Emerging: One variable discussed; limited or no storage impact mentioned; no conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes the purpose of the Domain Name System (DNS)?
A) It encrypts data sent between a browser and a web server
B) It translates domain names into IP addresses
C) It stores web pages on a server for fast retrieval
D) It assigns IP addresses to devices that join a network
practice_questions.marks: B) It translates domain names into IP addresses [1 mark]

practice_questions.text:
Identify the protocol and the path in the following URL:
https://www.example.co.uk/revision/networks
practice_questions.marks: Protocol: https (accept https://). Path: /revision/networks. Both parts must be correct to gain the mark. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'URL'.
practice_questions.marks: A URL (Uniform Resource Locator) is the complete address [1] used to locate a specific resource on the web, consisting of a protocol, domain name and optional path [1]. [2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the sequence of steps that occur when a user types 'https://bbc.co.uk' into a web browser for the first time, up to and including the browser receiving the IP address of the server.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
- The browser checks its own cache; since this is the first visit, no cached IP is found. [1]
- The request is sent to a DNS resolver (typically the ISP's DNS server), which also checks its cache. [1]
- The resolver contacts the root name server, which directs it to the relevant TLD server (.co.uk), which then directs it to the authoritative name server for bbc.co.uk, which returns the IP address. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between HTTP and HTTPS. In your answer, describe the security implications of using each protocol when logging in to an online account.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks:
HTTP:
- HTTP transmits data in plain text, so any attacker who intercepts packets can read the contents. [1]
- Using HTTP for a login would expose the username and password to anyone who intercepts the network traffic. [1]
HTTPS:
- HTTPS uses TLS encryption; the data is scrambled before transmission and can only be decrypted by the intended recipient. [1]
- Even if a packet is intercepted, the attacker sees only unreadable encrypted data, protecting login credentials. [1]

practice_questions.text:
Discuss the impact of the World Wide Web on education and learning.

In your answer, consider both the benefits the web brings to students and teachers, and the problems it can cause.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument with developed benefits (access to information, online learning platforms, teacher resources, collaboration tools, accessibility for remote learners) and developed problems (misinformation and unreliable sources, distraction and reduced concentration, digital divide where not all students have internet access, data privacy concerns); reasoned conclusion about net impact.
Secure: At least two developed benefits and two developed problems; conclusion present.
Developing: Arguments listed but not equally developed; conclusion limited.
Emerging: Simple one-sided statements.

practice_questions.text:
A web form asks a user to enter their age. The age must be a whole number between 5 and 18. Which validation check would reject the value 200?
A) Presence check
B) Format check
C) Length check
D) Range check
practice_questions.marks: D) Range check [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between validation and verification.
practice_questions.marks:
Validation: checks that data is sensible / in the correct format / within expected bounds (done by the program) [1].
Verification: checks that data was entered correctly / matches what was intended, e.g. double entry (done by a human or comparison system) [1].

practice_questions.text: A student registers for a website. Describe two validation checks that could be applied to the password field, which must be 8 to 20 characters long and must not be empty.
practice_questions.marks:
Presence check: ensures the field is not left blank / rejects empty string [1 + 1 development].
Length check: ensures the password is between 8 and 20 characters long / rejects passwords shorter than 8 or longer than 20 [1 + 1 development].
Mastering: Two distinct checks named and applied to the specific scenario.
Secure: Two checks named, one applied to scenario.
Developing: One check named and applied.
Emerging: One check named only.

practice_questions.text: Write a pseudocode algorithm that asks the user to enter a month number (1 to 12). Keep asking until a valid number is entered, then output 'Valid month'.
practice_questions.type: 6 marks — Write an Algorithm in Pseudocode
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: INPUT before loop, REPEAT...UNTIL or WHILE loop, correct condition (month < 1 OR month > 12), re-prompt inside loop, OUTPUT after loop — 5-6 marks.
Secure: Logic correct but minor keyword issue — 3-4 marks.
Developing: Loop present but condition or structure flawed — 2 marks.
Emerging: Some keywords used — 1 mark.
Model:
INPUT month
WHILE month < 1 OR month > 12
  OUTPUT "Enter a number between 1 and 12"
  INPUT month
END WHILE
OUTPUT "Valid month"

practice_questions.text: Explain two advantages of using a high-level programming language over assembly language when developing a payroll application.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks per advantage:
- Readability: high-level code resembles English / easier for other programmers to maintain / faster to write and debug [1 + 1].
- Portability: the same code can run on Windows, Mac and Linux with little modification / assembly code is tied to a specific processor architecture [1 + 1].
- Productivity: high-level abstractions (e.g. built-in string operations, libraries) mean less code to write for the same task [1 + 1].
Mastering: Two distinct advantages, each developed with a contrast to assembly.
Secure: Two advantages, one developed.
Developing: One developed advantage.
Emerging: One simple valid point.

practice_questions.text: A school database system is used to store student records. Discuss the importance of using both validation and verification to maintain data quality in the system.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains validation (at least two named checks applied to student records, e.g. range check on year group, presence check on name) AND verification (double entry for password or email; proofreading for imported records); acknowledges limitation of validation (cannot catch plausible-but-wrong data like a wrong year group); shows understanding that both are needed together; reaches a justified conclusion about combined use.
Secure: Both techniques explained with examples from the context; one limitation acknowledged.
Developing: Both techniques described without scenario application, or one technique well developed.
Emerging: One technique identified.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following correctly defines 1 kilobyte in a base-2 (binary) prefix system?
A) 1000 bytes
B) 1024 bits
C) 1024 bytes
D) 1000 bits
practice_questions.marks: C) 1024 bytes [1 mark]. This course uses base-2 prefixes; 1 kilobyte = 2^10 = 1024 bytes.

practice_questions.text: State the difference between lossy and lossless compression.
practice_questions.marks: Lossy compression permanently removes some data to reduce file size and the original cannot be fully recovered [1]. Lossless compression reduces file size without losing any data, allowing the original to be reconstructed exactly [1].

practice_questions.text: A 150 MB video file is compressed to 15 MB using lossy compression. Calculate the compression ratio.
practice_questions.marks: Compression ratio = original size ÷ compressed size [1 mark for formula]. 150 ÷ 15 = 10 [1 mark for calculation]. Compression ratio = 10:1 [1 mark for expressing as a ratio].

practice_questions.text: A hard drive has a capacity of 2 TB. Convert this to GB.
Explain why lossy compression is used for MP3 audio files but lossless compression is used for ZIP archives.
practice_questions.marks: Lossy compression discards some audio data that the ear is unlikely to notice (such as very high or very low frequencies, or quieter sounds masked by louder ones) [1], producing a much smaller file that is acceptable for casual listening [1]. A ZIP archive contains text, software or other data where every bit must be preserved exactly — removing any data would corrupt the file or make software fail to execute [1], so lossless compression is used to reduce size while guaranteeing that the original can be perfectly reconstructed [1]. Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Compare lossy and lossless compression techniques. In your answer, refer to how each works, the compression ratios typically achieved, and suitable use cases for each.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Accurate explanation of how each works (lossy discards perceptually unimportant data; lossless encodes patterns more efficiently e.g. run-length encoding), explicit comparison of typical ratios (lossy often 10:1 or more; lossless typically 2:1 to 5:1), correct use cases contrasted (lossy for streaming/social media; lossless for documents/software/master files), and a justified conclusion about when each is preferable.
Secure: Both techniques explained correctly, at least two explicit contrasts, suitable use cases given.
Developing: Both techniques defined but comparison is implicit; use cases may be partially correct.
Emerging: One technique described; limited or no comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Which IDE tool pauses program execution at a specific line so the programmer can inspect variable values?
A) Syntax error detection
B) Memory inspector
C) Breakpoint
D) Code editor
practice_questions.marks: C) Breakpoint [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State the difference between a compiler and an interpreter.
practice_questions.marks:
Compiler: translates the entire program at once / produces a standalone executable [1].
Interpreter: translates and executes the program one line at a time / requires source code at runtime [1].

practice_questions.text:
A student writes the following Python code:

x = 10
y = 0
print(x / y)

Identify the type of error this will produce and explain why.
practice_questions.marks:
Runtime error [1] because the code is syntactically correct and will pass translation [1], but dividing by zero causes the program to crash during execution [1]. A syntax or logic error would not apply here since the grammar is valid and the logic of dividing x by y is what was intended [1].
Mastering: Correct error type, explained with both why it is not syntax and why it occurs at runtime.
Secure: Correct error type with one valid reason.
Developing: Correct error type without explanation.
Emerging: Partially correct.

practice_questions.text: Describe what happens during the lexical analysis and syntax analysis stages of compilation.
practice_questions.marks:
Lexical analysis: source code is broken into tokens (keywords, identifiers, operators) [1]; comments and whitespace are removed [1].
Syntax analysis: tokens are checked against the grammar rules of the language [1]; a parse tree is built / syntax errors are identified and reported [1].
Award up to 3 marks from the four marking points above.

practice_questions.text: Explain two advantages of using an IDE compared to a plain text editor when writing a program.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks per advantage:
- Syntax error detection highlights mistakes in real time / before running, saving time finding typos [1 + 1].
- Debugger and breakpoints allow step-by-step execution / makes finding logical and runtime errors much faster than reading code manually [1 + 1].
- Variable watch shows values at each step / removes need to add temporary print statements to inspect variables [1 + 1].
Mastering: Two distinct advantages, each developed.
Secure: Two advantages, one developed.
Developing: One developed advantage.
Emerging: One simple relevant point.

practice_questions.text: Compare how a compiler and an interpreter handle errors. Discuss which approach is more useful when a programmer is still developing and testing their code.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explicit contrast of error handling (compiler reports all errors after full translation; interpreter stops at the first error, identifying the exact line); argues interpreter is more useful during development (immediate feedback, easier to locate the specific error line, no recompile step); acknowledges compiler advantage for final release (faster execution, no source code needed); justified conclusion — 5-6 marks.
Secure: One contrast and one argument for interpreter advantage, some development — 3-4 marks.
Developing: Correct description of one translator's error handling — 2 marks.
Emerging: A relevant point about one translator — 1 mark.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a brute-force attack?
A) Tricking a user into revealing their password by impersonating a trusted organisation
B) Flooding a server with traffic until it cannot respond to legitimate users
C) Systematically trying every possible password combination until the correct one is found
D) Inserting SQL commands into a form field to manipulate a database
practice_questions.marks: C) Systematically trying every possible password combination until the correct one is found [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by a Denial of Service (DoS) attack.
practice_questions.marks: A DoS attack floods a server or network with excessive traffic so that it becomes overwhelmed and cannot respond to legitimate users. [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe how SQL injection can allow an attacker to bypass a login system.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 3 marks:
- SQL injection involves entering malicious SQL code into a login form field instead of a normal username or password. [1]
- If the application does not validate or sanitise input, the SQL command is executed directly by the database. [1]
- This can trick the database into returning all user records or bypassing the password check entirely, granting access without valid credentials. [1]

practice_questions.text: Explain how two-factor authentication (2FA) reduces the risk of a brute-force attack being successful.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks:
- A brute-force attack attempts to discover a password by trying every possible combination. [1]
- Even if the attacker eventually guesses the correct password, 2FA requires a second verification step, such as a one-time code sent to the user's mobile device. [1]
- The attacker does not have access to the second factor, so they cannot complete the login even with the correct password. [1]
- This makes brute-force attacks ineffective in isolation because a password alone is not sufficient to gain access. [1]

practice_questions.text:
A hospital stores sensitive patient records in a database accessible via a web portal. A security consultant has recommended penetration testing and encryption as two key defences.

Explain how each of these defences protects the hospital's data, referring to specific threats each defence counters.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear explanation of both defences linked to specific threats (penetration testing: identifies SQL injection/authentication vulnerabilities before attackers; encryption: counters data interception and protects stolen data at rest); explicit connection between defence mechanism and the threat it counters.
Secure: Both defences explained with threat references; connection between mechanism and threat present but may lack one dimension.
Developing: Describes both defences but links to specific threats are vague or missing for one.
Emerging: Names the defences without explaining how they work.

practice_questions.text:
Cybersecurity threats are an increasing concern for individuals, businesses and governments.

Discuss the impact of cybersecurity threats on society. In your answer, consider the effects on both individuals and organisations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced discussion with developed impacts on individuals (financial loss, identity theft, loss of privacy, psychological harm from ransomware) and developed impacts on organisations (reputational damage, financial cost of attacks and recovery, legal liability under data protection law, disruption to critical services); may reference high-profile attack types (ransomware on NHS, DDoS on financial services); reasoned conclusion about scale and societal response.
Secure: At least two developed individual impacts and two developed organisational impacts; conclusion present.
Developing: Arguments listed on one side or the other without equal development; limited conclusion.
Emerging: Simple statements about harmful effects.
